82	### The compiled runtime
83	
84	`fortress run` compiles no Fortress source. It runs the jars of the program and of the library on the JVM. A jar holds JVM class files:
85	
86	- the component's functions, objects and traits;
87	- its closures;
88	- one dispatch method for each overloaded name. It tests the run-time types of all the arguments, from the most specific declaration to the least specific. Walk also chooses at run time.
89	
90	A generic declaration is compiled once, as a template class. The first time that a program uses an instantiation, such as `Box[\RR64\]`, the class loader makes its class. It copies the template's bytecode, puts in the static arguments, and loads the result. A static argument is a type, or a size as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`. These classes are never on disk. C# specialises generics in this way. Java erases them.
91	
92	The class loader is code of this tree that the revival changes, so a failure while a class loads can be its defect (`references/compiler.md`).
93	
94	HotSpot, the JVM's compiler, then compiles the hot bytecode to machine code. A number is a boxed object, also inside a specialised class: `RR64` is the class `FRR64`. An array is a library object, read and written through its `get` and `put` methods.
95	
96	### The caches
97	
98	A run keeps the results of its phases in the caches, so that a later run can reuse them. The caches are folders in `default_repository/caches/`, or in a private caches folder that a run names. An entry is one file in a cache, written for one source file.
99	
100	- `interpreter_parsed_cache/`: walk's parsed tree of each file, `X-<hash>.tfi` for an api and `X-<hash>.tfs` for a component.
101	- `interpreter_cache/`: walk's tree of each component after the phases. Walk loads it back and interprets it. The entry is a text dump of the tree. It starts `(Component @"`.
102	- `analyzed_cache/`: the results of the phases that `fortress compile` reuses.
103	- `bytecode_cache/`: one jar for each compiled component.
104	
105	In the first three caches, `<hash>` is a hash of the source's absolute path, and the entry holds that path. So the entries of a tree copied to another path must be renamed and rewritten. `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh` does this (`references/worktrees.md`).
106	
107	`references/build-and-caches.md` says when a run reuses an entry, and when the build empties the caches.
108	
109	### Parallelism and mutable state
110	
111	Fortress evaluates in parallel by default, not in Java's left-to-right order. The iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments and operands of a call can run at once. A loop is sequential only if every generator is `seq(...)`. The parallel parts run as tasks on a work-stealing pool, the fork/join pool of Doug Lea (a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sets its number of threads. Tasks, transactions and the pool are built twice, independently: for walk in `interpreter/evaluator/tasks/`, and for the compiled path in `runtimeSystem/`.
112	
113	`x = e` declares an immutable variable. `var x: T = e` and `x: T := e` declare a mutable one, and `x := e` assigns to it (`Specification/basic/variables.tex`). These are Scala's `val` and `var`, or Swift's `let` and `var`. A field is immutable unless it is declared with `var`. A value object is a tuple, `()`, or an object whose declaration, or a trait that it extends, has the `value` modifier, as the library's numbers, characters and booleans do. It has only immutable fields and value semantics, like a Swift `struct`. Nothing refuses a `var` field in a value object, so give it none. Any other object, except a function, is a reference object, like an instance of a Swift class. Each construction makes a new reference object, distinct from all others (`Specification/basic/objects.tex:24-33`).
114	
115	Parallel code stays free of races in these ways:
116	
117	- Most data is immutable.
118	- A big operator, such as `SUM` or `BIG MAX`, combines the results of its tasks, as OpenMP's reduction clause does. No task writes a shared accumulator. The specification's reduction variables are not built.
119	- A write to shared state goes inside an `atomic` block. This is software transactional memory, like Haskell's `atomically` (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex`). The programmer writes `atomic`; the compiler adds none.
120	- Tasks can write different elements of one array in parallel (`Specification/basic/memory-model.tex`, "Programming Discipline").
121	
122	So `acc := acc + x` inside a parallel `for`, with no `atomic`, is a race. The suites run at four threads, once each, so a race can show in them. A passing run does not prove that there is none.
123	
124	Inside an `atomic` block, the compiled code tracks each mutable variable that the block reads or writes, an object's `var` field among them. From the switch-over, it also tracks each array element that the block reads or writes (`references/compiler.md`).
125	
126	An `exit` out of an `atomic` block loses the block's writes, on both paths (ledger row 1039). Set a flag in the block, and exit after the block.

128	## Fortress as a language
129	
130	Each point below corrects an assumption from a language that you know. `references/tests-writing.md` gives the form of a program.
131	
132	- **Dispatch is on every argument, at run time.** A call chooses among overloads by the run-time types of all its arguments, as in Julia, not by static types as in Java. The checker accepts two overloads only if their parameter types exclude each other, one is strictly more specific, or a third covers their meet. The more specific one's return type must fit the other's: the Return Type Rule. Walk checks part of this at load.
133	- **Functional methods.** A method with `self` among its parameters is called `f(x)`, not `x.f()`. It overloads with top-level functions. Most operators are declared so: `opr +(self, other: T): T`. A functional method's name is reserved in every program that imports it, so do not name a variable after it. One type must not have a dotted and a functional method of the same name.
134	- **Traits and objects, no classes.** A trait has methods and abstract fields, and extends several traits. An object is a leaf. `excludes {A, B}` says that no value has both types. `comprises {A, B}` says that every value has a listed type, near Scala's `sealed`. No type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. This exclusion rule is why the number types are flat (below).
135	- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (a `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`, but a `ZZ` where it is one of a numeral type's numbers: `references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
136	- **Numbers are siblings, not a tower.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`. None is a subtype of another, unlike Haskell's classes or Java's widening. A wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A conversion does not change which declaration runs when one already fits. A numeral is the one exception: it can run a more specific declaration that its coercion reaches. Overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`, but an expression of numerals alone folds exactly (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"). The algebra is self-typed traits, such as `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` with `+`, not monoids over an operator parameter. `references/library.md` gives the rest: ranges, wrapping, `SUM`.
137	- **Loops and reductions are library code.** `for`, comprehensions and `SUM` call the library's generators and reductions (`references/library.md`).
138	- **Juxtaposition is an operator, and whitespace counts.** `f x` applies a function. Otherwise juxtaposition is an operator that the library overloads: `2 x` multiplies, and `"a" "b"` concatenates. How three juxtaposed items group depends on their types, unlike in Haskell. An infix operator has whitespace on both sides or on neither: `a -b` is a static error. Precedence is partial: `a + b ∪ c` needs parentheses.
139	- **Specified, but not built:** dimensions and units, `property` declarations, regions and complex numbers. Some constructs run only under walk (`references/compiler.md`).

4	: Script that runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library, on the `FortressLibrary` component and the apis that it imports, and prints the errors in a table: `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`. Its total is the checker count.
5	
6	**distance stage**
7	: Stage of the gate that runs the compiled checker over fourteen components of the interpreter's library, `FortressLibrary` among them, runs each of the checker's steps on each component whatever the earlier steps report, and prints the errors in a table. Your brief gives its command when you need it.
8	
9	The code of this area is in these directories:
10	
11	- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
12	- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
13	- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.
14	
15	The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.
16	
17	## What the two paths share
18	
19	After the phases, each path has its own code for these:
20	
21	- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
22	- Number natives: walk's glue classes, in `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`Int.java`, `Long.java`).
23	- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
24	- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.
25	
26	Both paths run the helpers, the public static methods of classes under `nativeHelpers/`.
27	
28	The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.
29	
30	## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over
31	
32	The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.
33	
34	Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: the switch-over deletes them, and their tests stay. Two exceptions (P-37): its numeral types and coercions follow `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", and a brief may ask to declare each built-in number type as one `value object`, the form that both libraries are to take. If a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is wrong, fix the helper's Java, even if the prelude binds it, and leave the prelude's text: its binding gives the fix. Change with it a compiled test that pinned the old result.
35	
36	## What the compiled path cannot compile yet
37	
38	For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:
39	
40	- `spawn`;
41	- an object expression;
42	- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.
43	
44	It compiles a local function as a closure, also one that calls itself or another local function of its block. It refuses these forms (ledger row 304):
45	
46	- a local function with static parameters of its own: 'Can't compile a local function with static parameters of its own yet';
47	- two local functions of one name in a block: 'Can't compile overloaded local functions yet';
48	- a local function with the `atomic` modifier: 'Can't compile a local function with this modifier yet'.
49	
50	A type assumption `e asif T` has the value of `e`, but the call around it chooses its declaration as if `e` were a `T`, a supertype of `e`'s type (`Specification/basic/expressions/type-annotation.tex`). The code generator compiles one at a dotted call's receiver, at a call of a functional method or an overloaded function whose every argument is an assumption, and elsewhere as the value of `e`. It refuses these forms (ledger row 818):
51	
52	- a call of a functional method or an overloaded function with an assumption at some of its arguments but not all: 'Can't compile a dispatched call whose arguments are not all type assumptions';
53	- a generic method on an assumed receiver: 'Can't compile a type assumption at the receiver of a generic method yet';
54	- a call of an overloaded generic function with an assumption at an argument: 'Can't compile a type assumption at a call of an overloaded generic function yet'.
55	
56	It also refuses a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose own header or `extends` entry has a `where` clause, and emits nothing for the clause. A call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, links, but dies at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError` (ledger row 867). `compiler_tests/XXXWhereVariableCallCompiled.test` records it: copy its form for such a call. The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private`, `abstract` and `test`, such as `override` (ledger row 650). A trait or object that extends a generic trait compiles with `Any` as the static argument. With `Bottom`, `Self` or an abbreviated type there, the code generator refuses the declaration. An abbreviated type is a short form, such as `RR64[3]` for an array type. With a tuple that holds `Any` there, the code generator crashes (ledger row 889).
57	
58	The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.
59	
60	Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).
61	
62	## What the code generator does
63	
64	- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
65	- It runs a program's own `coerce` from a numeral once for each place where the numeral is written, in the component class's static initializer, except where the place's type names a type parameter (below). The runtime initializes the class of each component that the program's classes name before `run()`, in one task. So a coercion's output comes before the program's first line, and the parallel parts of a coercion's body run one after another there. A coercion that raises stops the program before `run()`. A test of a coercion that raises sets `run_exits_nonzero=true` (`tests-writing.md`).
66	- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
67	- The `value` modifier adds the mark interface `ValueObjectMark` to the object's class. The compiled `SEQV` (`nativeHelpers/equality.java`) reads the mark. The modifier does not inline or unbox the fields.
68	- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet. If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):
69	
70	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:array is stored as' 'positions:array design'
71	
72	## The runtime
73	
74	- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes and for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417). Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
75	- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`), and an object's `var` field in a cell that the object holds. Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches. From the switch-over, it also tracks each element of the one library's arrays, by array and index: `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressArrayStore.java` calls the transaction's methods `TXReadSlot` and `TXWriteSlot`. Walk does not run this class, so test an edit of it with `ArrayStoreJUTest`, beside it.
76	
77	## Natives
78	
79	`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.
80	
81	A body `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")` binds one such method, a helper, too. In a compile, at the parse, the compiled path, and not walk, rewrites the body as a call of the method through a generated `import java`, with `self` first in a trait or object (`compiler/BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java`). The checker then checks the declaration against the method's Java signature. In a compile, it reads `int` as `ZZ32`, `long` as `ZZ64`, `float` as `RR32`, `double` as `RR64`, `boolean` as `Boolean`, `String` as `JavaString`, `BigInteger` as `ZZ` and `Object` as `Any` (`NamingCzar.fortressTypeForForeignJavaType`). The compile stops in these cases:
82	
83	- If the string is in that package but names no public static method: 'builtinPrimitive names no static helper: …'.
84	- If the string names a glue class or anything else outside that package: 'Variable builtinPrimitive is not defined.'
85	- If the declaration has a varargs parameter: the same message (ledger row 849).
86	- If the declaration is a local function or a method of an object expression: the same message. The rewrite reaches only a component's declarations and the members of its traits and objects (ledger row 865).
87	
88	The rewrite runs only in a JVM that has made a Fortress repository of the compiled path, the compiler's store of components, not this git repository. Walk's repository switches it off again. `fortress compile` makes one, and so do `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` and `typecheck` (`Shell.compilerPhases`). `fortress parse` and `fortress api` make none, so they rewrite a body only after a compile in the same JVM (ledger row 882). Alone, they pass a misspelt helper. Test a binding with `compile`. In a suite, the result of `parse` or `api` depends on whether a compile ran earlier in the same JVM.
89	
90	To test a helper on the compiled path, write a compiled test whose own declarations bind it, as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperBindingCompiled.fss` does. Until the switch-over, a compiled test cannot reach the interpreter's library's bindings.
91	
92	The count stage and the distance stage check the interpreter's library with the same rewrite. There, the checker differs from a compile in these ways:
93	
94	- A string that names a glue class, or a declaration with a varargs parameter, does not stop the check. The body stays a call of `builtinPrimitive`, typed at the declared result type, and no Java signature checks it (ledger row 849).
95	- The checker reads a helper's Java types as the interpreter's library's types: `String` as `String`, not `JavaString`, and the rest as in a compile.
96	- A component that imports a DSL grammar is parsed by other code (`GraphRepository.syntaxExpand`), which does not rewrite its bindings. So, as for a glue class, no Java signature checks them.
97	- The count stage checks only the `FortressLibrary` component's bindings. A binding of another component, as `FortressBuiltin`'s, only the distance stage checks.
98	
99	The checker, in a compile and in both stages, reads `int` as `NN32` or `Char`, and `long` as `NN64`, only for six transfer helpers with fixed names (`NamingCzar.java:373-384`, `:494-503`). Where a binding gives a parameter, `self` or the result the type `NN32`, `NN64` or `Char`, or a parameter or `self` the type `UnsignedLong` (the one library's object that extends `NN64`), and the helper has `int` or `long` there, the rewrite passes that value through the matching transfer helper. A result declared `UnsignedLong` gets none. `self` gets a transfer helper only in a method of one of these four types itself. The transfer helpers return their argument unchanged. So the checker accepts such a binding whatever helper it names, a signed one included, as `simpleIntArith.intLT` for `NN32`'s `<`. If you move a binding over these types onto a helper, test it on both paths at values where a signed and an unsigned reading differ (2^31 and above for `NN32`, 2^63 and above for `NN64`), as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Compiled.fss` and `tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Walk.fss` do. If the class has more than one method of the helper's name and number of parameters, the rewrite adds no transfer helper. The checker then reports 'Could not check call to function builtinPrimitive_<Class>_<method>', followed by '… is not applicable to an argument of type …'.
100	
101	The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method. In the count stage and the distance stage, a type maps only if the interpreter's library declares it. So there, a binding stops its component if any method of its helper's class has a type that only the compiler's prelude declares. The distance stage then counts the component as a stopped target. `nativeHelpers/systemOps` is such a class: its `getArgs` answers `StringVector`, so the message is 'FortressBuiltin.StringVector is undefined.' (F-321). Bind a helper of another class.
102	
103	## Traps of the compiled path
104	
105	- The compiler's prelude declares `print`, `println` and `String`'s `||` at `Object`, not `Any` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:37`, `:55`, `:61`). So until the switch-over, the checker refuses a generic that prints a value of a type parameter written without a bound, or concatenates it onto a `String`. The message names `Object`, as 'Object->() is not applicable to an argument of type T.' does for `println`. In such a generic of a compiled program or test, write `T extends Object`. The generic then takes no tuple, function or `()`. The one library declares these operations at `Any` or `String`, so do not change its text for this limit. The prelude's `||` takes the string first only, so `c || s` for a `Character` value `c` is refused (ledger row 965). Put a string first, as `("" || c) || s`.
106	- A `try`'s `forbid` clause lists exception types: an exception of a listed type that no `catch` clause took is wrapped in a `ForbiddenException`, which the `try` throws. A `try`'s `finally` clause does not run when one of these leaves the `try` block: an `exit`, an exception that no `catch` clause takes, or the `ForbiddenException` that the `try` throws (ledger row 890). So write no compiled program that relies on `finally` after an exception or an `exit` leaves the `try`. A test that needs it is an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`). A `try` whose block can throw, with a `finally` clause and no `catch` or `forbid` clause, fails with a `VerifyError` at class load (ledger row 891).
107	- To fork is to run as tasks that can run at once. A call's arguments and an operator's operands fork, as the rule says, where two or more of them are calls, written `f(x)`, of functions that the program declares. So write no compiled program that relies on the order in which its arguments are evaluated. Until the switch-over, the calls written in the compiler's prelude do not fork, so a compiled `SUM` runs one body at a time (ledger row 982). A compiled parallel `for` runs its bodies at once: use it in a test of parallelism.
108	- An `atomic` block (`atomic do ... end`) or atomic expression (`atomic e`, as `atomic 1`), a `try` or a `label` block as a call's argument after the first, as `f(k, atomic do ... end)`, fails with a `VerifyError` at class load, unless the arguments fork (ledger row 322). So does a `try` as an operator's operand after the first (ledger row 526). Bind its value in a statement of its own.
109	- Numerals and sizes depart from `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways:
110	  - At a place whose type names a type parameter of its generic declaration, a numeral's coercion runs at each evaluation (ledger row 957). If the body needs the value at one instance only, bind it once, at a top-level variable whose type names no type parameter.
111	  - Until the switch-over, `RR64` converts only an `RR32` and a numeral, and `RR32` only a numeral. So a `ZZ32` value where an `RR64` is expected is refused (ledger row 442). Write `i.asRR64` for a `ZZ32` value `i`.
112	  - The body block of a function with a declared return type dies at run time, with `NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerBuiltin$v`, in two cases: it ends in a numeral after a local declaration, or it ends in a tuple with a numeral element (ledger rows 1014, 1030). Bind each such numeral to a typed variable first, and write the variable in its place.
113	  - A numeral with a radix point at a place that fixes no type, which rounds to an infinity at `RR64`, gives `Infinity`, as under walk (ledger row 980). Assert no value for it in a test.
114	  - A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, raises a `java.lang.Error` that no `catch` sees (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.
115	  - As a `typecase`'s selector, a numeral keeps its own type, as `NaturalNumeral[\1,10,7\]`, so `typecase 7 of ZZ32 => ...` is refused as unreachable (ledger row 963). Bind the selector to a variable first, as `x = 7`, then write `typecase x of ...`.
116	  - A `label` block that ends in a numeral, where an `exit ... with` gives the block a `ZZ32` value, stops the code generator: 'Error trying to close method scope' (ledger row 340). Bind the numeral to a typed variable first, as `none: ZZ32 = -1`, and end the block with the variable.
117	  - At a place that fixes a type (`revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"), the checker refuses an atomic expression whose value is a numeral, as `atomic if c then 1 else 0 end`, and `atomic 1` fails the JVM's verification (ledger row 1043). Write `atomic do ... end`.
118	- An `exit` that runs after its `label` block has completed, from a function made in the block, ends a compiled program with the Java exception `LabelExit`, which no `catch` clause takes. Under walk, a `catch` clause of the library's `LabelException` takes it. The rules do not settle which is right (ledger row 1041).
119	- Where an object overloads an inherited functional method by declarations of its own, and `self` is not the first parameter, the compiled dispatch method tests the receiver's type where it should test the other argument's. A call then dies with `ClassCastException` (ledger row 573). Where the receiver has the parameter type of one of the object's own declarations, the call runs that declaration whatever the argument (ledger row 1038). Put `self` first in such overloads.
120	- On the compiled path, two `value` objects with a `var` field, built alike, are not strictly equivalent: `V(1) === V(1)` is `false` (ledger row 112).
121	- A reference to a generic function with one declaration, as `count[\F extends Object\](b: Box[\F\]): ZZ32`, takes its instance from the arrow type that receives it. Where the receiving type is not an arrow type, as in `p(count)` for `p(x: Any)`, the compile passes and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError` (ledger row 1012). Write the static argument there, as `p(count[\ZZ32\])`. The checker refuses a reference to a name with several declarations of which one is generic, unless one without static parameters fits the receiving arrow type (ledger row 1009). Pass a function of one declaration that calls the name.
122	- Where the initialiser of a top-level variable `b` assigns to a top-level `var a`, a compiled read of `a` before the first read of `b` gives the old value (ledger row 1011). Read `b` before you read `a`.
123	- A `typecase` tuple pattern with an untyped binder, as `(x, y: ZZ32)`, stops the code generator: 'typcase match failure!' (ledger row 964). Give each binder a type.
124	- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
125	- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
126	- A clean link does not prove that every call has its method. These die at run time with `NoSuchMethodError`:
127	  - a call of a functional method of an object that a trait's `comprises` clause lists, on a value whose static type is the object. An example is `num(R)`, where `trait Q comprises { R }` declares `abstract num(self): ZZ32` and `object R extends Q` gives its body. Call it through a value typed as the trait, as `q: Q = R` and then `num(q)` (ledger row 815);
128	  - a read of an exported object's value parameter, from a component that imports the api, where the exporting component names the parameter otherwise than the api. A value parameter is a parameter of the object's constructor, and also a field. An example is `Np(3).a`, where the api declares `object Np(a: ZZ32)` and the component `object Np(z: ZZ32)`. The export check compares no value parameter's name. Give each value parameter the api's name (ledger row 839);
129	  - an assignment from outside an object to its `var` field, of a value whose static type is strictly below the field's type, as `c.t := High` for `trait T`, `object Cell(var t: T)` and `object High extends T`. Bind the value at the field's type first, as `h: T = High` (ledger row 1053).

131	## The checker's gaps
132	
133	- Overloads: in its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays. The paths differ on `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects. The checker refuses it, because `Box[\Bottom\]` lies in both domains, and walk loads it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 786).
134	- The Return Type Rule: the checker refuses a pair of declarations that the rule accepts: a generic declaration beside one without static parameters whose domain is a tuple of object types, as `ident[\T\](x: T): T` beside `ident(x: (Circle, Circle)): (Circle, Circle)`, `Circle` an object (ledger row 1048). Walk loads and runs the pair.
135	- A tie: where two generic candidates fit a call equally, the checker sorts the candidates and keeps the first. The sort's order varies with what the same JVM compiled before. So the call's static type, or a crash, 'V is not in the kind env', can change with the order of the suite (ledger rows 499, 1046, 1047). If a compiled test passes alone and fails in the suite, look for such a tie first.
136	- Inheritance: the checker refuses an object that reaches a generic self-typed trait's method along two paths, one through a trait that declares the method again at the same parameter types: 'There are multiple declarations of m with the same parameter type'. Without static parameters it accepts the form. Walk runs the lower trait's declaration. The specification's section "Method Declarations" (`Specification/basic/traits.tex`) does not settle which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 1037).
137	- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the compiled code does not check it. A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:
138	  - at a dotted call, a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable;
139	  - at a type's use, a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable;
140	  - a static argument written at a top-level call, against its parameter's bound (ledger row 470).
141	- A reduction without its static argument, whose bound names its parameter, such as `SUM`: the checker reports a type error in its body as the big operator's refusal, 'is not applicable to an argument of type ()' (ledger row 1015). Write the static argument to read the body's error.
142	- Imports: `import A.{...}`, with the three dots written, imports every name of `A`. The overloading check also reads `A`'s declarations of a name that the component imports by name from another api. So `import A.{...}` beside `import B.{ pick }`, where both apis declare `pick(x: P)`, is refused: 'There are multiple declarations of pick' (ledger row 813). Leave the name out of the whole import, as `import A.{...} except { pick }`.
143	- An `except` clause leaves out each identifier that it lists, on both paths. Neither path leaves out an infix operator that it lists. So where a component lists `-` in `except` and declares its own `-` at the api's parameter types, the code generator stops. Walk runs the component's own `-` (ledger row 814).
144	- Conditional extension: the condition holds while the checker checks the `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member. It does not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).
145	- A `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, as `NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]` or `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`: at a call, the checker gives the variable a fresh size or type, equal only to itself. Two values passed in one call get two. A fresh type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints. The variable is in scope in the trait, except in its `extends` and `excludes` clauses. The checker gives no fresh type where it meets the trait as a supertype of another type. Where a generic type that the clause lists, as `List[\E\]`, gives the body of a member of the trait, the code generator crashes: 'E is not in the kind env' (ledger row 812). Where the variable is a size, a compiled call that passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected fails the JVM's verification (ledger row 307). Departures: a fresh type also under a function type's result (ledger row 751), none for an extender that the clause does not list (ledger row 752), and a crash at a call, from outside the trait, of a member whose type names the variable (ledger row 756).

147	## The `fortress` commands
148	
149	`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.
150	
151	- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
152	- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
153	- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
154	- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.
155	
156	## Running
157	
158	    cd ProjectFortress
159	    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
160	    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
161	    ../bin/fortress run P [args]

163	A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.

166	- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead.

195	## The checker's time
196	
197	This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.
198	
199	The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 80 to 180 seconds, more under load. It can run past the Bash tool's 120-second limit, so run it in the background (`session.md`). It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.
200	
201	The checker checks every api first, and the component only if no api has an error. In each api or component, it stops at the first of its stages that finds errors. The stages run in this order (`compiler/StaticChecker.java`, `checkCompilationUnit`):
202	
203	1. The type hierarchy and the type check.
204	2. The overloading check, which also compares the overloads' return types.
205	3. In the component only, the export check (`library.md`, "Designing a change").
206	
207	So the count misses the errors of the later stages, and a fix of an early error can raise it.
208	
209	The table's rows tell a clean run from a run that the checker did not finish:
210	
211	- `#total 0` and `#locations 0`: the checker reached the component and found no error.
212	- `#stopped`, in place of `#total` and `#locations`: the errors came from a phase before the checker, such as the parse. The checker reported none and did not reach the component. The script exits 1, and the gate reads the table as red.
213	- `#crash`: the first crash of the overloading check that the run survived, or `none`.
214	
215	If the run printed no error total and was not clean, the script writes no table and exits 1.
216	
217	The checker's results are the programs that it accepts and refuses, and each error with its text and its place. On the interpreter's library, a change keeps the results the same if both of these hold:
218	
219	- The two tables are equal: `diff` prints nothing.
220	- The two `run.txt` files are equal after you replace each run's own tree path with one word, such as `TREE`. Any difference fails.
221	
222	A node's hash starts from its class name, so an order in the output, such as the apis' checks, does not vary from run to run. A moved order is a difference: keep the old order, or report it.
223	
224	`Walker`, in the generated `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, is split into methods under 8,000 bytes of bytecode. HotSpot does not compile a longer method, and the walker runs on every node. `MethodSizeJUTest` fails if a method of the build grows past the limit, except the methods that its source lists in `listed(...)` entries. Run it alone with `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=MethodSizeJUTest`. If a method of `Walker` fails, lower `WALKER_CASES_PER_METHOD` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/ScalaAstGenerator.java`. If another method fails, split it under the limit. List it only if nothing in the checker or a compiled run calls it, with its size and what runs it, and name it in your report.
225	
226	The timing is a smoke test, to catch a slowdown of several times. One run of each tree is enough. A small difference, or one within the noise from run to run, is not a finding. In your report, say what you saw, and do not analyse it.
227

1	# The interpreter (walk)
2	
3	Walk's code is in `interpreter/`:
4	
5	- `evaluator/`: the tree walker.
6	- `env/`: the environments, which map names to values, and the wrappers that load components and apis.
7	- `rewrite/`: walk's own rewrite of the tree.
8	- `glue/`: the natives.
9	
10	## How walk evaluates a program
11	
12	After the phases (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"), walk rewrites each component in `interpreter/rewrite/`: it gives each reference to a name the lexical depth of its declaration. The evaluator looks up the name by that depth. The compiled path has no such rewrite.
13	
14	At a call of a generic function, walk infers the static arguments from the run-time types of the arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction`). Each static parameter gets an interval, from a lower to an upper bound, in a `LatticeIntervalMap` (`useful/`). A type in the domain of an arrow type, such as `T` in `T -> ZZ32`, is contravariant. So its bounds go into the dual map, `LatticeIntervalMapDual`: the same table, with the order reversed. `MakeInferenceSpecific` then makes the inferences more specific, in practice only in the dual map.
15	
16	A generic function passed as a value takes its instance from the arrow type that receives it: a parameter, a local variable declared with the type, or an assignment. So `app(half, v)` runs for `half[\nat n\](x: Vector[\RR64,n\]): Vector[\RR64,n\]` and `app(f: Vector[\RR64,3\] -> Vector[\RR64,3\], v: Vector[\RR64,3\])`. Where no arrow type receives it, or the arrow type leaves a static parameter open, the value stays generic. Walk then infers the static arguments at each application. The checker refuses such a program, so do not rely on this in a program for both paths (ledger row 1021). Walk departs from this in three cases:
17	
18	- An immutable top-level variable of arrow type, an object's field of arrow type and a declared arrow return type keep the generic value. So for a top-level `g: Vector[\RR64,3\] -> Vector[\RR64,3\] = half`, `g(w)` runs for a `w: Vector[\RR64,2\]` (ledger rows 1019, 1036).
19	- For `appT[\T\](f: T -> T, x: T)`, `appT(half, v)` is refused, 'Unification error': `v` fixes `T` by its run-time type. Write the static argument, as `appT(half[\3\], v)` (ledger row 1018).
20	- A generic function declared inside a block stops at its declaration, whether it is passed or not: 'Missing type T' (ledger row 1020). Declare it at the top level.
21	
22	Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. Walk has no static types, so it cannot choose statically. The expected-failure tests `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss` and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss` record the difference.
23	
24	Walk departs from the rules of `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways, until each fix lands. A test of one of these cases asserts the rules' answer, as an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`), unless the case says otherwise.
25	
26	- A numeral with a radix point keeps only one of its leading zeros, so a coercion over `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` gets `n` = 2 for `00.5`, not 3 (ledger row 960).
27	- A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, is a `ZZ64` (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.
28	- A numeral in a call whose other argument is a variable declared `Any` converts by that value's run-time type, not to its default. So `a = 0` is `true` for `a: Any` that holds a zero `NN32`, where the rules' answer is `false` (ledger row 1016). To compare as the rules do, bind the numeral first, as `z = 0`, then write `a = z`.
29	- A numeral with a radix point at a place that fixes no type, which rounds to an infinity at `RR64`, its default, gives `Infinity`, with no error, on both paths (ledger row 980). The rules do not say whether it is an error, so assert no value for it in a test.
30	- A numeral type written in a `comprises` clause loads and runs, as `trait T comprises { NaturalNumeral[\1, 10, 3\] } end` does (ledger row 981). The rules refuse it, as the compiled checker does, and as walk does at load in an `extends` clause or as a static argument: 'NaturalNumeral cannot be written in a program except as a parameter's type.'
31	- A body with a declared return type is not converted by coercion, except a numeral: `r(): Wide = NarrowOf(3)` returns the `NarrowOf` (ledger row 387). Write the value at the declared type.
32	
33	Walk also departs from the rules at these bindings:
34	
35	- The right side of a top-level tuple binding runs once for each name and once more: `(first, second) = pairOnce()` runs `pairOnce` three times (ledger row 1026). Bind the call to one name, as `pair = pairOnce()`, then write `(first, second) = pair`.
36	- A `var` declared in a block with an array type and bound to an array literal, as `var t: ZZ32[2] = [5 6]`, is immutable: 'Cannot assign to immutable t' (ledger row 1024). Bind the literal to an immutable name, and initialize the `var` from it.
37	- An array literal assigned to a variable, as `t := [7 8]`, is not built into an array: 'Type mismatch assigning' (ledger row 1025). Bind the literal to an immutable name of the array type, and assign the name.
38	
39	## Where a fix of walk belongs
40	
41	Both paths run the same desugaring phases. Inside them, switches in `Shell.java` decide which desugarings run. Walk turns off these desugarings, which the compiled path runs:
42	
43	- coercion;
44	- chained comparisons;
45	- compound and tuple assignment, and subscripts;
46	- case expressions, typecase and type ascription;
47	- the marking of a bodiless declaration as abstract.
48	
49	Walk evaluates those nodes itself, in `interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java` (`forChainExpr`, `forAssignment`, `forCaseExpr`, `forTypecase`, `forAsExpr`). It converts by coercion at dispatch, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchWithCoercion`. So if walk is wrong on one of these nodes, fix the evaluator, not the desugarer.
50	
51	Walk keeps each choice of a declaration in a dispatch cache, except a choice that asked a program's own type for its numeral coercion: that coercion's `where` clause can take one numeral and refuse another. If you change how a numeral chooses a declaration, check that the cache's key (`Numerals.Keys`) tells apart the calls that now choose differently.
52	
53	An edit of a phase that both paths run, or of the desugaring switches, can change both paths. An edit under `interpreter/` changes walk only.
54	
55	## What walk checks
56	
57	Walk does not check static types (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"). The commands that stop after a phase, and `unparse`, use the compiler's prelude and the compiled path's desugaring switches (`compiler.md`, "The `fortress` commands"). So `fortress typecheck` does not check a walk program, and `desugar` or `unparse` does not print the tree that walk runs. That tree is the component's entry in `interpreter_cache/` (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").
58	
59	Under walk, the disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses a program's own top-level type that has the name of a type of `FortressLibrary`, such as `Index` or `Indexed`: "Type name may refer to: Index, FortressLibrary.Index". Give such a type another name.
60	
61	At load, walk checks the overload sets, some `comprises` clauses, inherited abstract methods and `override` declarations. It lifts each object expression to the top level as an object, which takes the static parameters of an enclosing generic function, and checks it as an object. It checks a trait or object with static parameters once, through a stand-in: one type for all its instances, with a symbolic type for each static parameter (`symbolicInstance` in `interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java`). Through the stand-in, it does not check two functional methods whose parameter types mention a symbolic type. It makes no stand-in, and so checks nothing through one, for a declaration with an `opr` static parameter, or where its static parameters, `where` clause or `extends` clause raise an error at the symbolic types. It refuses:
62	
63	- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap. For every pair of functions of which at least one is generic, it checks the overloading rules of `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language", on their declared domains (`revival-changes.md`, "Dispatch and overloading"): the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule. So it refuses two whose declared domains are equal. The message names the rule: "fails because their parameter lists have the same types", "fails the Return Type Rule" or "fails the Meet Rule". Walk keeps the team's check and messages for the pairs below. The team's check looks for a position where the two parameter types neither nest nor exclude. If a parameter type there mentions a static parameter, the message is "at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types". If neither does, it is "are unrelated (neither subtype, excludes, nor equal) and no excluding pair is present". The pairs:
64	  - a pair with a varargs parameter;
65	  - a pair whose parameter lists differ in length, only where one of them has a varargs parameter. Walk checks no other pair of lists of different lengths;
66	  - a pair that is neither two generic declarations, nor a generic one beside a plain one, nor a generic function beside a generic trait's or object's functional method that has no static parameters of its own;
67	  - the instances of an explicit instantiation.
68	
69	  Where it reads exclusion over the whole tuple of parameter types, at the instance that the equalities force, it reads two parameter types that still mention a static parameter as excluding only where no instances of the two can meet. Walk departs from the rules in these cases:
70	  - At load, it does not check two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains. It compares them at each call, on the instance that the call makes. So such a pair that breaks the rules loads, and a call can fail with "Cannot find definition for method" (ledger row 780).
71	  - It refuses two generic functional methods whose declared domains lie one inside the other, in a type without static parameters (ledger row 779).
72	  - It refuses a pair whose overlap it finds only through an instance of a supertype, also where a third declaration covers the overlap (ledger row 539).
73	  - It refuses overloads on two instantiations of one generic type, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])` (ledger row 416).
74	  - Its parameter-by-parameter check reads an object type over a static parameter as excluding a type that one of its instances is or extends. So it loads `g[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: ZZ32)` beside `g(x: Box[\ZZ32\], y: Any)`, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 788).
75	  - It reads no `where` clause when it reads exclusion over the whole tuple. So it refuses such a pair where one declaration has a `where` clause of its own (ledger row 787).
76	  - It does not refuse a type that extends a self-typed trait `T[\A\]` and is not an `A` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). A call that both `T`'s operator and another declaration fit then runs one of them, without an ambiguity error (ledger row 893). Make each type that extends `T[\A\]` an `A`.
77	  - It loads a generic top-level function whose declared domain lies inside that of a self-typed trait's functional method of the same name, where the Return Type Rule holds. The checker refuses every top-level function more specific than a functional method of its name, a check that the specification does not state: '… is more specific than the declaration of the functional method' (ledger row 894).
78	  - It loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 806).
79	  - It loads a type that provides two functional symbolic operators, such as two `||`, that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`). The checker refuses the pair (ledger row 611).
80	  - Beside a generic declaration, it does not judge by the Return Type Rule a declaration without static parameters that writes no return type and whose parameter types are object types, as `NN32` is in walk's library: `pick[\T extends Number\](a: T): ZZ32 = 1` beside `pick(a: NN32) = "two"` loads (ledger row 1044). Write the return type.
81	  - It reads no `comprises` clause for the Return Type Rule. So it refuses a valid pair over a trait that comprises one object, as `pickFirst[\T extends Number\](a: T, b: T): T` beside `pickFirst(a: ZZ64, b: ZZ64): ZZ64`, where `ZZ64` comprises the one object `Long` (ledger row 550).
82	  - It loads a pair that breaks the Return Type Rule over an arrow type, as `ident[\T\](x: T): T` beside `ident(x: Circle -> Circle): (Circle -> Circle)`: a function of type `Any -> Circle` is also a `Circle -> Circle`, and at that instance the generic one returns `Any -> Circle`. The checker refuses the pair (ledger row 1049).
83	
84	  The paths differ on `f[\T extends { K, R[\T\] }\](x: T)` beside `f(x: Z)`, where `K comprises { A, B, C }`, `Z excludes { A, B }`, and `C` is an object that extends `Z` but not `R`. Walk refuses the pair: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker reads the bounds, finds that no value lies in both domains, and accepts it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 713).
85	- two functional methods that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods in a type that provides both, where their name is an identifier or an operator named by a word, as `MAX`.
86	- an overloaded function with one parameter of type `T`, where `T extends Any` is written: `f[\T extends Any\](x: T)`.
87	- an extender that a `comprises` clause of the program's main component does not allow. Walk does not yet check the library's clauses, another component's clauses or an object expression's clauses. Where a listed type names a bounded type `where`-clause variable, as `NBox[\E\]` in `comprises { NBox[\E\] } where [\E extends Number\]`, walk ignores the variable's bound, and runs `NBox[\String\]` (ledger row 754). In another declaration's bound, it takes a name equal to the variable's as the variable (ledger row 778).
88	- a trait whose `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, where a member's declared type names the variable: "Missing type E" (ledger row 755).
89	- an object or object expression without static parameters that inherits an abstract method and does not define it. Bodies define it if they are at or below its parameter types and together cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk also refuses where its search for a cover does not settle: at a cycle of `comprises` clauses, at a symbolic type, or beyond 10,000 steps or 4,096 combinations of listed types. It also refuses a valid object whose one body for the method has a static parameter of its own (ledger row 728).
90	- a declaration with the modifier `override`, in a trait, object or object expression, that overrides no declaration that its type's immediate supertraits provide. An `override` at an inherited declaration's own parameter types overrides nothing. At an instance of a generic trait above a declared object, equal parameter types count as overridden. Walk does not read all the bounds of the static parameters in two cases:
91	  - an object expression, which takes its static parameters from the function around it;
92	  - a generic trait or object that extends a type under a `where` clause.
93	
94	  In these cases, walk does not refuse an `override` if the inherited declaration's parameter types mention a static parameter and differ from the `override`'s.
95	
96	So a library edit can stop every program at load, if it does one of these:
97	
98	- adds an overload;
99	- leaves an inherited abstract method that no bodies cover, covers it only by a body with a static parameter of its own, or covers it by bodies whose cover walk's search cannot settle;
100	- adds an `override` that overrides nothing;
101	- gives a member a type that names its trait's `comprises`-clause variable, as `E` in `AnyList`;
102	- names, in a `builtinPrimitive` string, a helper that walk refuses ("Natives").
103	
104	Walk checks a program's declarations against the library's only when it analyses the library, not when it loads the library's entries from the cache (ledger row 342). So a program that walk refuses with an empty cache runs with a filled one. Deleting the program's own entries does not bring the check back. To see such a refusal, run with an empty cache, as `COLD_CACHE=1` gives `harness-one.sh`.
105	
106	Walk compares no component with the apis that it exports. So a component that leaves out an api member, or declares it at another header, loads and runs under walk. The compiled export check refuses it (ledger row 841). `library.md`, "Designing a change", gives the step that runs the check on each component.
107	
108	`tests-writing.md` says how a test names a refusal at load.
109	
110	Walk's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that varies from run to run. On one core, the order is fixed for a given library, but a library edit can change it. Do not pin or compare this order. The harness reads only that an `XXX` test fails.
111	
112	## Natives
113	
114	The library binds each of walk's natives by a declaration whose body is `builtinPrimitive("…")`. The string names one of these:
115	
116	- A glue class, as `com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X`, in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. A glue class takes walk's `FValue` objects, so the compiled path cannot use it.
117	- A helper: a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, as `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.<method>`. `interpreter/glue/StaticNativeApp.java` calls it by reflection, with a method's `self` first. The compiled path calls it too (`compiler.md`, "Natives"). Most bindings name a helper. The others name a glue class. F-299 counts both kinds (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
118	
119	Walk carries each declared type of a helper's binding in one Java type:
120	
121	- `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `Char` in `int`; `ZZ64` and `NN64` in `long`; `RR64` and `Float`, the library's object that extends `RR64`, in `double`; `RR32` in `float`; `Boolean` in `boolean`;
122	- `FlatString` and `JavaString` in `String`, and `String` too, except as a parameter other than `self`; `ZZ` in `BigInteger`; `()` in `void`; `JavaBufferedWriter` and `JavaBufferedReader`, the library's writer and reader traits, in `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressBufferedWriter` and `FortressBufferedReader`, which the checker reads back as the two traits.
123	
124	In a method, walk carries `self` by the type that declares the method:
125	
126	- a type of the list above, except `JavaString` and `()`, in the same Java type, but `FlatString` only where it is the library's own;
127	- the library's objects that extend number types, not the glue classes of the same names: `Int` (`ZZ32`) in `int`, `Long` (`ZZ64`) and `UnsignedLong` (`NN64`) in `long`, and `BigNum` (`ZZ`) in `BigInteger`.
128	
129	A program can give its own type the name `FlatString` or `JavaString`. Walk tells the library's `FlatString` by the component that declares it, so a program's own type of either name carries no `self`. But walk carries a parameter declared at such a type in `String`, by the type's name alone, and does not refuse the binding. The native then receives the name of the type, not the value's text (ledger row 877). Give a program's own type another name.
130	
131	Walk refuses a helper's binding at load in these cases. The message names the string, and contains the words below, which a `load_exception_contains` key can match:
132	
133	- The class or the method does not exist: 'not found' or 'names no static method of'.
134	- The result type, or a parameter type other than `self`'s, is not carried by the first list: 'no Java type carries the declared'.
135	- The binding is in a method of a type that the second list does not name, as a program's own object: 'no Java type carries T, the type of self.', with the type's name as T. Match ', the type of self.' to tell it from the refusal above.
136	- No method of that name, or more than one, has exactly the Java types of the lists, with `self`'s first in a method: 'has no overload that fits the declaration's types', or 'overloads that fit'.
137	
138	The check has two gaps:
139	
140	- Walk checks the binding of a dotted method of a generic trait or object only when the program makes an instance, at run time. So a program that makes no instance loads. One that makes an instance stops there with the same message, as an `InterpreterBug` (ledger row 864). Test such a binding with a program that makes an instance.
141	- Walk reads the type that declares the method, not the type of the value. So a program's object that extends `ZZ32` loads. A call of a method of `ZZ32` that binds a helper then stops with 'getInt not implemented for FOrdinaryObject' (ledger row 551).
142	
143	A glue class bound over `String`, and a helper bound in a method of `String` as `self`, receive the wrong text for a `CatString`: the name of the type, not its characters (ledger row 846). `||` builds a `CatString` when the joined string is longer than `maxLeafSize`, 32 characters by default. A `||` of string literals folds into one literal, a `FlatString`, so a test that needs a `CatString` joins a literal with a variable. Bind such a native over `FlatString`, and beside it an overload over `String` that passes `s.asFlatString`, as `printlnWithThread` does (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4640-4644`). In a method of `String`, call that overload with `self`.
144	
145	An `import java` written in a `.fss` file is wired under walk but unfinished, and no test uses it. The compiled path's generated `import java` (`compiler.md`, "Natives") is not this one.
146	
147	A glue class raises a Fortress exception that a `catch` sees by throwing a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object. `Int.overflow()` in `interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java` makes one, and its callers throw it:
148	
149	    FObject f = (FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException);
150	    return new FortressError(f);
151	
152	A helper runs on both paths, so it raises an exception as compiled code does: `throw Utility.makeFortressException("fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero")` (`compiler/runtimeValues/Utility.java`). A message can follow as a second argument, as in `nativeHelpers/runtime.java:53`, which raises `FailCalled`. The string names the compiler's prelude's class for the exception. Under walk, that class does not load, and `StaticNativeApp` raises the interpreter's library's object of the same name in its place, without the message. So raise from a helper only an exception that both libraries declare as an object, as `DivisionByZero`, `IntegerOverflow` and `FailCalled`. `DIV`, `REM` and `MOD` by zero on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64` raise `DivisionByZero` in this way, on both paths. So no division, remainder or modulus by zero on these types ends the run. A `catch` sees no other Java exception, so any other Java exception of a native, a glue class's included, ends the run.
153	
154	## Running a program
155	
156	    bin/fortress P.fss
157	
158	- If the run stops on an error, it prints the error and the Fortress stack under `Context:`. The hint below them names `-debug interpreter`, which shows nothing more. To see the Java stack too, run `bin/fortress -debug stacktrace P.fss`.
159	- Walk searches for imports in the current directory first (`build-and-caches.md`, "Name resolution").
160	- If `JAVA_FLAGS` is not set, `bin/fortress` uses `-Xmx256m -Xss32m`. Your setup gives a 4 GB heap, and the test harness uses 768 MB. A test can pass at two of these heaps and die at the third. If you claim that a run fails near a memory limit, measure the claim at 256 MB: run with `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx256m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"`.
161	- Your setup sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, the size of the pool, to 1 (`SKILL.md`, "Parallelism and mutable state"). If it is unset, the pool has half the CPUs.
162	- A small program takes about 8 s with cold caches, and about 4 s with warm caches.
163	- Do not take or record a timing of walk. Do not edit anything to make walk faster.
164	- To check a build, run `bin/fortress explorations/claude_demo.fss`. It prints `SUM[i <- 1#100] i = 5050` among its lines, and exits 0. `ProjectFortress/hello.fss` runs only on the compiled path.

166	## The model program
167	
168	MicroGPT runs only under walk, by hand, never in the gate. Check the model when your brief asks for it: run your tree's `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]`. `<work-dir>` is a folder under your tree's `tmp/`, and `threads` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, 1 by default. The script runs the quick pair at once, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`: two forward and backward passes each, against the reference values, in about 56 s for both. Each starts from an empty private cache and writes `<work-dir>/<name>.txt`. Read its `VERDICT:` line and its last line, `rc=`.
169	
170	- Add the word `full` only if your brief asks for it. It runs the full pair, `MicroGptFlatCheck.fss` and `MicroGptAplCheck.fss`, with 40 checks each and a 90-minute timeout.
171	- If you change a line of the model, put the change in your report as a diff.

1	# The report and the record
2	
3	## What every report holds
4	
5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
6	
7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22	
23	## At a point to report
24	
25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
26	- Then finish the work.
27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
28	
29	## Timings and citations
30	
31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
35	
36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
37	
38	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
39	
40	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
41	
42	## The gap ledger
43	
44	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
45	
46	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
47	
48	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
49	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
50	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
51	
52	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
53	
54	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
55	
56	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
57	
58	## Reading the record
59	
60	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
61	
62	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
63	
64	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
65	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
66	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
67	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
68	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
69	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
70	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
71	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
72	
73	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
74	
75	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
76	
77	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
78	
79	## Writing to the record
80	
81	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
82	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
83	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
84	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
85	  - what it means for the work;
86	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
87	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
88	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
89	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
90	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
91	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
92	
93	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
94	
95	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
96	
97	To add a row:
98	
99	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
100	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
101	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
102	
103	To change a row:
104	
105	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
106	- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
107	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
108	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
109	- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

112	
113	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.

If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
